lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Syracuse, Sicily. Two hundred and twelve BC. The Romans are inside the city.

lines.speaker: SOLD
lines.text: You! Old man! The general wants you. Get up!

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Not now. Do not disturb my circles!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You are the student of the greatest mind of the ancient world. And this is his last day. Go back twenty years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You're twelve, and your mother sends you to deliver bread to a strange old man near the harbor.

lines.speaker: MOM
lines.text: Give him the bread, and make sure he eats it. His servants say he forgets.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Sir? Your bread. Sir? Why are you drawing circles in the ashes?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Because I have no sand tray, and the fire went out. Come here. Tell me: which is bigger, this circle, or this square?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: The square?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Wrong! But a good guess. Come back tomorrow, and I'll show you why.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: His name is Archimedes. He's about fifty-five, a relative of the king, and the most famous mathematician alive. You never deliver bread again. You become his student.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: I'm Kleon, the other apprentice. Rule one: when he's thinking, don't talk. Rule two: he's always thinking.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: One day, a message comes from King Hiero himself.

lines.speaker: HIERO
lines.text: I gave a goldsmith pure gold to make a crown for the gods. I think he kept some gold, and mixed in silver. Prove it, Archimedes. And don't damage the crown.

lines.speaker: GOLD
lines.text: Your Majesty, it's pure gold, I swear by every god in Sicily!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Master, how can you see inside a crown without breaking it?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: I don't know yet. I am going to take a bath and think.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He steps into a full bath, and the water spills over the edge. And he jumps out.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Eureka! Eureka! I have found it!

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Master! Your clothes! You're running through the streets with no clothes!

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Silver is lighter than gold, so the same weight of silver takes more space. A cheating crown will push out more water than the pure gold!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: But why not just weigh it?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: I did. Same weight! The trick is not the weight. It is the space the crown takes up.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The crown spills more water than the gold. The goldsmith is caught. This story was written down two hundred years later, so maybe it's true, and maybe it's too good to be true.

lines.speaker: HIERO
lines.text: Archimedes, they say you can move anything. Prove it. My new ship, the Syracusia, is too heavy for a hundred men to launch.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Give me a place to stand, Your Majesty, and I will move the Earth.

lines.speaker: CAPT
lines.text: The Earth? Sir, just move the boat. It's the biggest ship ever built.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He builds a system of pulleys and ropes. Then he sits down, alone, and slowly pulls.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: It's moving! The whole ship is moving!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Master, how? You're not even sweating!

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Every pulley halves the effort. Use enough of them, and one old man is stronger than a hundred.

lines.speaker: HIERO
lines.text: From this day on, Archimedes is to be believed in everything he says!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: On that same ship, sailors use a turning screw to pump water out of the hull. Farmers still use the Archimedes screw today.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Master, what are you counting now?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Grains of sand. How many grains would it take to fill the whole universe?

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: That's impossible. There are infinitely many.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: No, Kleon. Very many is not infinitely many. I need a number with sixty-three zeros. So I'll invent a new way to write big numbers.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And the circle from the first day? Why was it bigger than the square?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Watch. I draw a shape with six sides inside the circle. Then twelve. Then twenty-four, forty-eight, ninety-six. The closer they hug the circle, the better I can measure it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's how Archimedes trapped the number pi between two fractions: a little more than three and ten seventy-firsts, and a little less than three and one seventh. Engineers used his bounds for more than a thousand years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Then King Hiero dies, and Syracuse switches sides, from Rome to Carthage. In two-fourteen BC, a Roman army arrives.

lines.speaker: MARC
lines.text: Syracuse has old walls and an old mathematician. We attack from the land and the sea at once. Five days, and the city is ours.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Sixty Roman warships, with ladders on them! Master, what do we do?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Master, you're over seventy. Shouldn't you hide?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: At my age, hiding takes too long.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: We do geometry. Boys, bring the ropes. And the big hook.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: As the Roman ships reach the walls, giant wooden arms swing out over the water.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Lower it! Lower the claw! Now pull!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: An iron hook grabs a warship by the bow, lifts it out of the sea, and drops it.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Ha! Look at them swim!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Catapults hit the ships far out at sea. Smaller ones hit them up close. The Romans have nowhere to hide.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: The ladder ships! They're tying ships together to carry a ladder!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Drop the stones! Now! Break the ladder!

lines.speaker: MARC
lines.text: Are we going to keep fighting this geometrical giant, who plays catch with our ships?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Soon, if the Romans see so much as a rope or a beam over the wall, they turn and run. The siege drags on for two years.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Master, people in the market say you burn Roman ships with mirrors.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Do they? How clever of me.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Could we? If every soldier on the wall held a polished shield?

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: The sun is strong, but ships move. And the sky is not always clear. Try it, and tell me.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: No writer from the time mentions burning mirrors. The story appears centuries later. In two thousand and five, MIT students lit a model ship with a hundred and twenty-seven mirrors, but only after ten minutes of perfect sun on a ship that didn't move.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Two-twelve BC. The city celebrates a festival for Artemis. Wine, music, and tired guards.

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Listen. Do you hear that? Something on the wall.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ladders! The Romans are on the wall! Wake up! Wake up!

lines.speaker: KLEO
lines.text: Where's the master?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: In the courtyard, drawing. Where else? Come on!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: By morning, the Romans hold most of the city. General Marcellus looks down at Syracuse, and he weeps.

lines.speaker: MARC
lines.text: Find Archimedes. Bring him to me alive. No one touches him.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Master, we have to go! The soldiers are everywhere!

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: One moment. I am so close. Look at this figure.

lines.speaker: SOLD
lines.text: You! Old man! The general wants you. Get up!

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Not now. Do not disturb my circles!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The soldier doesn't know who he is. The greatest mind of the ancient world dies over a drawing in the sand. Some versions say so, at least. Even Plutarch tells three different stories.

lines.speaker: MARC
lines.text: Who did this? I gave an order! He was worth more than the whole city.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Marcellus gives Archimedes an honorable burial. On his tomb, as he wished: a sphere inside a cylinder. His proudest discovery.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A hundred and thirty-seven years later, the Roman orator Cicero comes to Syracuse and searches for the tomb.

lines.speaker: CIC
lines.text: Cut away these bushes. There! A sphere and a cylinder. The Syracusans had forgotten their own greatest citizen.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Then his books almost vanish too. In twelve twenty-nine, a monk scrapes the ink off an old copy of Archimedes and writes a prayer book on top of it.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: They erased him?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Almost. In nineteen-oh-six, a Danish scholar in Istanbul spots faint mathematics under the prayers. In nineteen ninety-eight, the book sells for two million dollars. Scientists scan it with X-rays.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Underneath is a lost book called The Method. Archimedes was slicing shapes into infinitely thin pieces: ideas close to calculus, almost two thousand years early.

lines.speaker: ARCH
lines.text: Very many is not infinitely many. But it is a beginning.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you'd been his student, which of his machines would you have built first? Tell me in the comments.
